query: For multi-component concentrated alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their strength and deformation or failure behavior, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the conditions over which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC CoCrNi-based multi-component alloys, increasing the degree of short-range order (SRO) enhances yield strength and strain-hardening capability by raising the stacking fault energy (SFE), which shifts the deformation mechanism from twinning to planar dislocation slip.
generation.material_initial_state: FCC CoCrNi-based alloy in a near-random solid solution (RSS) state with low initial SRO
generation.intervention: Controlled thermomechanical processing (e.g., sub-critical annealing at temperatures below full homogenization) to induce varying extents of SRO without triggering phase decomposition
generation.conditions: Applied to CoCrNi-based alloys (including non-equiatomic variants such as those modified with V) at temperatures where enthalpic interactions dominate over configurational entropy; testing should occur over strain rates and temperatures relevant to typical low-to-intermediate use conditions
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of local chemical order (SRO) and the associated modification of stacking fault energy (SFE)
generation.mechanism: SRO alters local atomic arrangements, increasing the energy barrier for dislocation movement by raising the SFE. This suppresses deformation twinning and promotes planar dislocation slip, leading to higher yield strength and an enhanced strain-hardening response
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys treated to induce higher SRO will exhibit a measurable increase in SFE, higher yield strength, and a deformation microstructure dominated by planar slip (with reduced twinning) compared to alloys processed to maintain a near-RSS state
generation.baseline: Alloys processed at high temperatures (e.g., 1100 °C) that approximate a random solid solution (RSS) with low SRO, lower SFE, and a higher tendency toward deformation twinning
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold in FCC CoCrNi-based alloys and their non-equiatomic derivatives within processing conditions that do not cause unwanted phase transformations. Its applicability to alloys with significantly different crystal structures or very high levels of elemental misfit may be limited
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between SRO degree and SFE, as well as the potential interplay with other strengthening mechanisms (e.g., grain boundary and solid-solution strengthening, especially with V addition), remains to be fully characterized

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of FCC CoCrNi-based alloy samples with identical compositions. Process one group by high-temperature annealing (yielding an RSS state) and another group by sub-critical annealing to promote SRO. Characterize the degree of SRO using atom probe tomography or suitable diffraction techniques, measure SFE via electron microscopy or related methods, and test mechanical properties (yield strength, strain hardening) along with detailed analysis of the deformation microstructure to identify slip modes.
measurements: Quantification of SRO (e.g., via atom probe tomography or XRD diffuse scattering)
Tensile testing to determine yield strength and strain-hardening rate
Microscopic examination (TEM/SEM) to assess the prevalence of planar slip versus deformation twinning
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with higher induced SRO do not exhibit an increased SFE, higher yield strength, and a deformation microstructure shifted towards planar slip (with a decreased frequency of twinning) relative to the RSS baseline, then the hypothesis is refuted

However, this RSS state is possible only at very high temperatures, where the degree of local chemical order (LCO) is negligible and the entropy term predominates the free energy reduction to dictate ideal mixing. Real-world HEAs are actually processed (annealed and homogenized) and used at relatively low temperatures,, where complex enthalpic interactions among various constituent elements come into play. Even the pioneering Cantor alloy, a face-centered cubic (FCC) SS close to random if annealed at 1100 °C, decomposes after long anneal at <900 °C. Appreciable chemical order has in fact been found in a number of HEAs. As such, HEAs, even when in the form of a single-phase SS, can be of a mixing entropy far below Sc,ideal.

As the temperature decreases, solute-solute interaction and mixing enthalpy (enthalpic contribution) predominate the Gibbs free energy and induce local ordering of the chemistry. Appreciable short-range order (SRO) has emerged in long-time annealed MPEAs and considerably affects dislocation slip and mechanical behavior (, ). As a salient feature pertaining to MPEAs, an intriguing question remains as to whether or how SRO affects the strongest size, maximum strength, and the underlying deformation mechanisms.
Within the numerous MPEA systems, the face-centered cubic (fcc) CrCoNi-based alloys have attracted extensive attention owing to their extraordinary mechanical properties, including high strength and ductility (, ).
